fields.features_heading: What Makes a DEI Survey Worth Answering
fields.features_subheading: A DEI survey, also called a diversity survey, asks how fairly people are treated and whether they belong, then compares teams.
fields.feature_1:
Statements sorted into themes

Sorts each statement under belonging, fairness, voice, or growth, then scores every theme on its own. Ask Emergent for a starting set of DEI survey questions, or paste in yours.
fields.feature_2:
Self-ID that never blocks a response

Makes every demographic question optional, with Prefer not to say and a box to self-describe. Someone who skips the whole section still submits the survey and counts in the totals.
fields.feature_3:
Identity kept apart from opinions

Saves self-ID answers in their own table, tied to each response through a random ID. Reports can split scores by demographic group, and nobody browsing the raw data sees a name.
fields.feature_4:
A minimum size on every cut

Hides any group with fewer answers than the minimum you set, such as 10, in every chart and export. Those responses stay in the company score but never show for that group.
fields.feature_5:
Gaps against the company score

Places each department's theme scores beside the company figure and flags any gap you choose, such as half a point. The department head then gets an email listing the lowest items.
fields.feature_6:
The survey app, in your GitHub

Exports the finished app to your GitHub repository on paid plans, with its question logic, reports, and response database. Run it on your own servers or keep editing in Emergent.

fields.usecase_heading: Four DEI Surveys, Built and Running
fields.tab_content_1:
Field Ops trails the company on belonging

Once a year, all 640 people at a logistics company rate 18 statements on belonging, fairness, voice, and growth. Each department's theme scores sit beside the company's. Field Ops scored 3.2 on belonging against 3.9 overall, and its department head got an email with the three lowest items.
fields.tab_content_2:
A skip option on every self-ID question

Every demographic question in the self-ID section is optional and offers Prefer not to say, plus a box to self-describe. Someone who skips all of it still submits the survey. Self-ID answers land in a separate table, linked to the survey answers by a random ID instead of a name.
fields.tab_content_3:
Groups under 10 answers stay off the report

Cut the results by location and shift, and each group's inclusion score appears with its answer count. Any group with fewer than 10 answers shows as hidden. Its answers still count toward the company total, but that slice never appears alone. The Reno night shift had 7 answers this round.
fields.tab_content_4:
Fairness scores, 90 days after the plan

The four fairness statements go back to every team 90 days after the action plans. Each team's June score sits beside its March score. Field Ops rose from 3.1 to 3.6, the biggest gain of any team, after its managers began posting open shifts to everyone at once.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a DEI Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan a DEI survey people answer honestly and leaders act on, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the results will change
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set the smallest group you will show
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the decisions the results should feed, such as how promotions are reviewed or how managers run team meetings. Write them down before drafting a single statement. People notice when a survey leads nowhere, and they answer the next one with less care.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Phrase each item as a statement on a 1-5 agreement scale, such as "I can disagree with my manager without worrying about it." Group the statements under four or five themes. Hold it to about 18 items, so the survey takes under 10 minutes.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Put the demographic questions at the end, mark each one optional, and offer Prefer not to say. Ask only about the groups you plan to report on. Every extra question shrinks the slices you can show and makes a small group easier to identify.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick a minimum answer count, such as 5 or 10, below which a group's results stay hidden. Apply it to every cut, including combinations like location and shift. Combined cuts shrink fast, and the minimum is what keeps a two-person group off the report.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write out who takes it, the statements and themes, the self-ID questions, the group minimum, and who sees which report. Emergent builds the survey with its own response database and reports. A later change, such as a fifth theme, takes one more message.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the survey with a short note on what is collected, who can read the results, and how small a group can be before it hides. Say plainly whether the survey is anonymous or confidential. Repeat the group minimum in every reminder email.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Rerun the items behind each plan
fields.howto_step_7_des: Once results are out, each leader picks one action for their lowest theme. Ninety days later, send only those statements to the same groups again. The two rounds side by side show whether the action moved anything people can feel.

og.headline: Build a DEI survey
og.alt: Build a DEI survey with Emergent

faq_plan.a: A DEI survey is an employee survey that measures diversity, equity, and inclusion inside a workplace. People rate statements about how fairly they are treated, then answer optional demographic questions so scores can be compared across groups. The goal is to find where one group's experience at work differs from the company's, not to count heads.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a DEI survey?
faq_plan.a: Start by deciding what the results should change, then write about 18 rated statements grouped under a few themes. Put an optional self-ID section at the end and set the smallest group a report may show. With Emergent's AI survey builder, you describe that plan in plain English and get the survey and its response database as one app.

faq_plan.q: Should DEI survey questions be rated statements or open-ended?
faq_plan.a: Use rated statements for nearly all of them, with one or two open-ended questions at the end. A 1-5 agreement scale gives every team a score you can compare between rounds. In a small team a turn of phrase can identify the writer. Give comments their own minimum before a group's written answers show.

faq_plan.q: When is the right time to send a diversity survey?
faq_plan.a: Send it in a quiet stretch, not the week after layoffs or performance reviews, when answers measure the news instead of the culture. Leave it open for 2 weeks with one or two reminders. People who are leaving are better asked in an exit survey, where the questions can turn to why they are going.

faq_plan.q: Can I start from a DEI survey template and edit it?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Ask Emergent for a starting DEI survey template, such as 18 statements under four themes with an optional self-ID section. Then change it by prompting, for example adding a theme on flexible work or raising the group minimum to 10. Emergent changes the survey and its dashboard together, and the reports follow the new questions.

faq_plan.q: Which topics should a DEI survey cover?
faq_plan.hint: What questions should you ask on a DEI survey?
faq_plan.a: Cover the parts of work where experience can differ between groups: belonging, whether pay and promotion decisions seem fair, whether people can speak up, and whether they see room to grow. Write two to five statements per topic, such as "Promotions here go to the people who earn them" under fairness. Ask self-ID questions only about groups you will report on.

faq_plan.q: How often should companies run DEI surveys?
faq_plan.a: Once a year suits the full survey, with a short pulse survey in between on the statements behind each action plan. Repeating the survey on a schedule is what shows movement: one round is a snapshot, and two give you a trend. Keep each statement word for word the same across rounds, or the scores stop being comparable.

faq_plan.q: What is the difference between an anonymous and a confidential DEI survey?
faq_plan.a: An anonymous survey keeps responses separate from every personal identifier, including the respondent's department. A confidential survey connects each response to personal information, such as an HRIS record, and certain administrators can identify respondents. Say which kind yours is in the first line.

faq_plan.q: How can I get more employees to answer a DEI survey?
faq_plan.a: Before you ask again, send a short note naming one action per theme from the last round. Keep the survey under 10 minutes on a phone, and keep any anonymity promise you make. Anonymity encourages candid responses, and it lifts participation too. Emergent sets no response caps on the survey it builds.

faq_plan.q: How is a DEI survey different from an engagement survey?
faq_plan.a: Run a DEI survey alongside an employee engagement survey, not in place of one: the DEI version asks whether the experience at work is the same for everyone. It relies on optional self-ID questions to compare groups, and it needs stricter rules on small groups. Emergent can build both from a plain-English prompt, each with its own response database.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a DEI Survey People Trust Enough to Answer', meta 'DEI Survey Builder With Confidential Results | Emergent' and hero 'Build a DEI survey with skippable self-ID questions, small groups hidden in reports, and answers in a database you own.' cover the whole job, not one feature.

intent.evidence: Definition up top (FAQ 1, features subheading), seven-step how-to 'How to Run a DEI Survey', themes and example statements ('I can disagree with my manager without worrying about it.', 'Promotions here go to the people who earn them'), and a builder angle the consultancy-heavy AMBER top 10 lacks.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: self-ID, Prefer not to say, group minimum, 'Reno night shift had 7 answers', anonymous vs confidential; table uses the library survey column.

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: 'Once a year, all 640 people at a logistics company rate 18 statements', 'Cut the results by location and shift', 'Pick a minimum answer count'.

craft.evidence: No blocking craft defect; list density (11 'A, B, and C' lists) and one ', so' ending recorded as notes.

voice.evidence: Concrete, unglamorous detail ('after its managers began posting open shifts to everyone at once', 'Field Ops scored 3.2 on belonging against 3.9 overall'); no AI tells.

truth.evidence: Unsourced statements of fact: FAQ 8 'An anonymous survey never records who answered, while a confidential one links each response to an ID and limits who can see that link.'; FAQ 10 'An employee engagement survey asks how committed and motivated people are overall'; FAQ 9 'a short note naming one action per theme earns more answers than any reminder'. None has a spec.domain_sources entry.

distinct.evidence: Own story (self-ID table, small-group suppression, 90-day fairness rerun); no sibling primary in a heading; engagement, pulse and exit surveys only linked in FAQ answers.

findings.quote: An anonymous survey never records who answered, while a confidential one links each response to an ID and limits who can see that link. Confidential answers can be joined to department or tenure without asking people for them.
findings.issue: Defines two professional survey terms as fact (and the meta title's 'Confidential Results' promise rests on them) with no spec.domain_sources entry for the anonymous vs confidential distinction.
findings.fix: Add the claim to plan.claims_to_source with a primary source that states the distinction (for example a survey-platform help article on anonymous vs confidential surveys) and quote it in domain_sources; keep the copy within what the source says, or cut the definition.

findings.quote: An employee engagement survey asks how committed and motivated people are overall
findings.issue: States what an engagement survey measures, a professional definition, with no domain source.
findings.fix: Source the engagement-survey definition (commitment/motivation) in domain_sources with a quote, or rephrase the answer around what the DEI survey does without defining the other survey type as fact.

findings.quote: a short note naming one action per theme earns more answers than any reminder

findings.fix: Recast as advice without the comparative effect ('Before you ask again, send a short note naming one action per theme.') or source it.
